newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leaders fail to agree on election.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leaders fail to agree on election.

text.p: Albania's two main parties met formally on Wednesday for the first time since they joined an interim government, but failed to agree on the form of early elections called to halt the slide towards chaos.

Tritan Shehu, leader of the Democratic Party of Albanian President Sali Berisha, said after meeting Socialist leader Fatos Nano's delegation that their failure to agree on what voting system to use did not affect the date of the poll, due by June 29.
The Democrats want a majority system while the Socialists are pressing for proportional representation.
"It was a consultative meeting to exchange information on the position of the two parties and we shall meet again in three to four days," Shehu told reporters.

Berisha agreed to share power with the Socialists in a nine-party National Reconciliation Government on March 9, as growing unrest following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes pushed the country to the brink of anarchy.

The Socialists, alleging fraud, withdrew late on polling day from general elections last May. The Democrats won 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament. International observers said the voting was flawed.
The Socialists won a commitment from Berisha for fresh elections as the price for joining the interim coalition.

They maintain that the situation in Albania, where unofficial estimates say up to a million weapons have been distributed after military arsenals were looted during the unrest, precludes normal campaigning and the only fair voting system is proportional representation.
The Democrats want to keep the system that enabled them to win so handsomely at the last election.
Berisha has been complaining that the salvation committees, citizens groups that sprung up in the south as anarchy swept the region, also prevent a free and fair vote and must be disbanded.
The Socialists say Berisha is only seeking the disbandment of the committees because they blame him for the collapse of the pyramid schemes and will organise voting against his party.

Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela, an independent close to the monarchist party, said earlier this week that the parties needed to agree on the form of the vote soon if the electoral law was to be passed by parliament as planned by May 15.
An early election is seen as crucial to beginning the long process of pacifying and rebuilding Albania.
Several hundred people have been killed in the past two months, many the victims of accidental or revenge shootings as lawlessness swept Europe's poorest state.
At least 22 people were reported killed in an explosion at a weapons depot outside Tirana early on Wednesday. A similar blast last week was blamed on youths trying to steal explosives.

In the southern city of Gjirokaster, the local police chief said residents hid in their homes on Wednesday as carloads of gunmen from a neighbouring village drove through the streets firing their weapons to protest at the killing of a kinsman.
